newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish February CPI good but not base for rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Polish February CPI good but not base for rate cut.

text.p: Polish inflation was slower than expected in February but the better figures are unlikely to prompt any rate moves by the central bank, now more concerned with credit growth and trade deficit, analysts said.

Polish consumer prices rose 1.1 percent in February against a 2.9 percent rise in January taking the year-on-year index down to 17.3 percent from 18.1 percent. The government target for 1997 in year-on-year terms is 13 percent.
"The February data is a nice surprise after the finance ministry said it expected February inflation at 1.6 percent," said Marek Zielinski, analyst at Bank Slaski SA.
A monthly Reuter poll among the country's 25 biggest banks showed last week the market expected February consumer price growth at 1.65 percent.

However, analysts said the inflation data, long one of the key factors in the central bank's interest rate decisions, became secondary to credit and trade gap growth amid concern Poland's balance of payments deficit may slip out of control. @

"It seems that the trade and broad money figures are now more important and that the central bank will keep nominal rates flat to curb credit and keep the trade deficit under control," said Andrzej Burliga, analyst at Bank Zachodni SA.
"There is likely to be a large gap between nominal rates and inflation but maybe this way they (the central bank and the finance ministry) will succeed in controlling the trade gap," he said.

Analysts expect the trade gap to rise to $12 billion in 1997 from $8.15 billion in 1996 -- a move which could erode the country's currency reserves needed to pay Poland's huge foreign debt. The reserves are now at a comfortable $18 billion.
The National Bank of Poland wants to help limit the trade deficit by cooling domestic demand, reflected in credit growth. The finance ministry supports that policy.

Personal credit showed some signs of slowing after the first two months of this year but still rose 5.7 percent against 1.8 percent growth of money supply in that period after a 108 percent jump in the whole of 1996.
Analysts said the NBP was unlikely soon to cut rates after it raised the obligatory reserve requirements for banks as of March to clamp down on credit action.

"I think that despite the good February CPI, we have to wait until mid-1997 for a move on rates because a near-term cut is unlikely after the NBP raised reserve requirements," said Piotr Las, analyst at Creditanstalt Securities in Warsaw.
"This would mean that, in line with what the NBP had been saying, real interest rates will keep growing with falling inflation," he said.
